Deniz O.lab_name: Nutrient Sensing group (Hietakangas lab), Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and Institute of Biotechnology, University of Helsinki (Helsinki, Finland)
Deniz O.role: Doctoral researcher in Ville Hietakangas's nutrient-sensing group in Helsinki, and first author of the fruit-fly study that found Spalt-related to be a stress-activated brake on mTORC1-driven growth
Deniz O.sub: Doctoral Researcher, Nutrient Sensing group, University of Helsinki
story: Onur Deniz was first author of a 2026 EMBO Journal study in fruit flies (DEN2026). When an animal runs short of nutrients it has to stop building new tissue and storing fat. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is the main switch for that building work. The study found that a transcription factor called Spalt-related (Salr), a protein that turns genes on and off, holds mTORC1-driven growth and fat storage back in the fat body, the fly organ that does the jobs of our liver and fat tissue.

Salr is switched on by the integrated stress response, a cell-wide alarm system that reacts to stress such as missing amino acids. It works side by side with FoxO, the better-known starvation regulator, rather than taking orders from it. So the fly has at least two separate brakes on growth that respond to different signals. The work was done in flies, and whether a similar Salr brake works in mammals was not tested here.

Deniz is listed as a doctoral researcher in the Nutrient Sensing group led by Ville Hietakangas at the University of Helsinki. The group page quotes Deniz's aim as finding new physiological regulators of nutrient sensing.

highlights.DEN2026: First author: identified Spalt-related as a brake on mTORC1-driven growth and fat storage in the fly fat body, switched on by the integrated stress response.

Hietakangas V.lab_name: Nutrient Sensing group, Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and Institute of Biotechnology (HiLIFE), University of Helsinki (Helsinki, Finland)
Hietakangas V.role: Professor of gene regulation at the University of Helsinki who uses fruit flies to study how animals sense nutrients and how diet controls growth, metabolism and stem cells
Hietakangas V.sub: Professor of Gene Regulation and group leader, MetaScale Centre of Excellence, University of Helsinki · postdoc with Stephen Cohen, EMBL Heidelberg and Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory, Singapore (papers 2007–2009) · doctoral work with Lea Sistonen, Turku Centre for Biotechnology, Turku (papers 2003–2005)
story: Ville Hietakangas was senior author of the 2026 fruit-fly study in this Atlas (DEN2026). It found that a transcription factor called Spalt-related (Salr) restrains mTORC1, the growth-control complex, when nutrients are scarce. Salr limits growth and fat storage in the fat body, the fly's equivalent of liver and fat tissue. It is switched on by the integrated stress response, a cell-wide alarm system, and works alongside FoxO rather than below it. The result adds a second, separate brake to the picture of how a starving animal stops growing. It was shown in flies only.

Hietakangas began in a very different area. Papers from 2003 to 2005 with Lea Sistonen at the Turku Centre for Biotechnology in Finland describe how heat shock factors, proteins that protect cells under stress, are controlled by chemical tags called SUMO. As a postdoc with Stephen Cohen, first at EMBL in Heidelberg and then at the Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory in Singapore, Hietakangas moved to growth signalling in flies. A 2007 Genes & Development paper showed that TOR complex 2, the second mTOR complex, acts as a booster that widens the range of AKT signalling, and that it matters most when the pathway is overactive, as in tumour-like overgrowth. In 2009 Hietakangas and Cohen wrote an Annual Review of Genetics overview of how nutrition controls tissue growth.

The Hietakangas group in Helsinki studies nutrient sensing: how cells read the animal's nutritional state and turn it into changes in gene activity, including sensing of sugar and the nutrient control of intestinal stem cells. The university presents this basic research as relevant to diabetes and fatty liver. Hietakangas is Professor of Gene Regulation at the Faculty of Biological and Environmental Sciences and the Institute of Biotechnology, and a group leader in the MetaScale Centre of Excellence.

highlights.DEN2026: Senior author: led the fly study showing that Spalt-related, switched on by the integrated stress response, restrains mTORC1-driven growth alongside FoxO.

Garami A.lab_name: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research (Basel, Switzerland)
Garami A.role: First author of the 2003 study, from George Thomas's group at the Friedrich Miescher Institute, showing that insulin switches on Rheb and that the TSC1-TSC2 complex switches it off
Garami A.sub: Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel (at the time of the study, 2003)
story: Attila Garami was first author of a 2003 Molecular Cell paper (GAR2003) that helped fix the order of steps above mTOR. Rheb is a small GTPase, a molecular switch that is on when it holds GTP and off when it holds GDP. The study showed that insulin raises the amount of active, GTP-loaded Rheb. The tumour-suppressor proteins TSC1 and TSC2 work together as Rheb's GAP, an enzyme that makes Rheb burn its GTP and so turns it off. Active Rheb in turn drives the signals that mTOR sends to S6K and 4E-BP, the proteins that boost protein synthesis.

Put together, this placed Rheb directly upstream of mTOR and directly downstream of TSC1-TSC2. It explained why losing TSC1 or TSC2, as in the disease tuberous sclerosis complex, leaves mTOR stuck on. The work used cultured cells and fruit-fly genetics.

The paper came from the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel, where Garami worked in George Thomas's group. A current position could not be confirmed from an official source, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.GAR2003: First author: showed that insulin activates Rheb and that TSC1-TSC2 acts as Rheb's off-switch, placing Rheb directly upstream of mTOR.

Garami A.note: Identity uncertain beyond the 2003 paper. A Szeged University PhD thesis (2006) by an Attila Garami on Leishmania mannose activation exists, and PubMed has Garami A with Ilg T on Leishmania (2000-2001); could be the same person (FMI postdoc), but no source ties them, so it is left out. Do not confuse with Andras Garami (Pecs, thermoregulation).

Um SH.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine (Suwon, South Korea)
Um SH.role: Molecular biologist at Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine whose work centres on the S6 kinases, and first author of the 2004 Nature study showing that mice without S6K1 resist obesity
Um SH.sub: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Suwon (papers 2012–2024) · Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel (2004)
story: Sung Hee Um was first author of a 2004 Nature paper (UMX2004) from the group of George Thomas at the Friedrich Miescher Institute in Basel. S6K1 is a kinase that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on when nutrients and insulin are plentiful. The team bred mice that lack S6K1 entirely. On a normal diet and on a high-fat diet these mice stayed lean as they aged and kept their insulin sensitivity, while normal mice grew fat. The knockout mice burned more fat and their fat cells stayed small.

The study matters because it ties one branch of mTORC1 output directly to weight gain and to insulin resistance, the first step towards type 2 diabetes. It was done in mice, so it shows what removing S6K1 does in a mammal, not what blocking it would do in people.

Um went on to lead work on the S6 kinases at the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, in Suwon, South Korea. As senior author in 2012, Um showed in mice that the sister kinase S6K2 restrains the liver's production of ketone bodies, the fuel made during fasting, by holding back the receptor PPAR-alpha. Later papers from the same department, in 2020 and 2024, found that S6K1 in the cells surrounding a tumour, especially macrophages, helps tumours build blood vessels and spread to the lung in mice.

highlights.UMX2004: First author: showed that mice lacking S6K1 resist age- and diet-induced obesity and stay more insulin sensitive.

Um SH.note: Current position at Sungkyunkwan taken from PubMed affiliations (latest 2024); no official faculty page found to confirm title. Link FMI 2004 to SKKU is the shared S6K1/S6K2 knockout-mouse topic.

Chen Xizi.lab_name: Yanhui Xu laboratory, Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Chen Xizi.role: Structural biologist in Yanhui Xu's group at Fudan University who was first author of the 2018 cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 and co-first author of an earlier structure of human mTORC1
Chen Xizi.sub: Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center and Institutes of Biomedical Sciences, Fudan University, Shanghai (papers 2016–2018, at the time of the study)
story: Xizi Chen was first author of the 2018 Cell Research paper (CHE2018) that gave the first close look at human mTORC2, the second of the two mTOR complexes. The team used cryo-electron microscopy, which freezes purified proteins in thin ice and builds a 3D model from many thousands of images, and reached 4.9 angstrom resolution. The complex is a hollow, diamond-like shape in which two copies of mTOR form the scaffold. The partner proteins Rictor and mSin1 sit right next to the spot where the drug rapamycin would bind. They block it, which explains at the level of shape why rapamycin hits mTORC1 but not mTORC2.

The structure also showed that Rictor and Raptor, the defining partner of mTORC1, use overlapping contacts on mTOR, so a single mTOR cannot belong to both complexes at once. These are results from purified human proteins, not from cells or animals.

Two years earlier Chen was one of four co-first authors of a 4.4 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC1 in Protein & Cell. The paper credits Chen with purifying the protein, running biochemical tests and helping with crosslinking mass spectrometry. Both papers came from Yanhui Xu's laboratory at Fudan University in Shanghai, in collaboration with Hong-Wei Wang's cryo-EM group at Tsinghua University. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.CHE2018: First author: solved the 4.9 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2, showing how Rictor and mSin1 block rapamycin binding.

Chen Xizi.note: Common surname; only the 2016 Protein & Cell and 2018 Cell Research papers (same lab) are tied to this person. Current position unknown.

Porstmann T.lab_name: Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory (Almut Schulze), Cancer Research UK London Research Institute (London, England, United Kingdom)
Porstmann T.role: Cell biologist who, as a researcher in Almut Schulze's laboratory at the Cancer Research UK London Research Institute, showed that the growth kinase Akt drives fat synthesis through SREBP and that this route runs through mTORC1
Porstmann T.sub: Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory, Cancer Research UK London Research Institute, London (papers 2005–2009, at the time of the study)
story: Thomas Porstmann was first author of a 2008 Cell Metabolism paper (POR2008) that connected two big ideas about cell growth. A growing cell has to make more membrane as well as more protein, and membranes are built from fats. SREBP is a family of transcription factors, proteins that switch on genes, and they control the genes for making fatty acids and cholesterol. The study showed in human cells that when the kinase Akt is switched on, the active form of SREBP1 builds up in the nucleus, and that this needs mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, stopped it.

Blocking SREBP did more than lower fat production. It also stopped Akt from making cells bigger, and in fruit flies loss of SREBP reduced cell and organ size. So mTORC1 also orders the lipids for new membranes, on top of speeding up protein production. The work was done in cultured cells and in flies.

The paper grew out of Porstmann's earlier first-author study in Oncogene (2005) in the same laboratory, which used gene-expression arrays to find that Akt switches on cholesterol and fatty acid enzymes through SREBP. In 2009 Porstmann and colleagues summarised the SREBP and mTORC1 link in a Biochemical Society Transactions review. All three papers list the Gene Expression Analysis Laboratory led by Almut Schulze at the Cancer Research UK London Research Institute, now part of the Francis Crick Institute. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.POR2008: First author: showed that Akt-driven activation of SREBP and fat synthesis needs mTORC1, and that SREBP is required for Akt to make cells grow.

Porstmann T.note: PubMed also has a Thomas Porstmann at ETH Zurich (Markus Stoffel lab, 2013, liver lipid metabolism, PMIDs 23416070, 23860498); topic fits but no shared co-author, so left out. Older Porstmann T records (1990s Berlin immunology, Crohn's GP2 autoantibodies) are a different person. The statement that the LRI is now part of the Crick is general knowledge, not from a page opened in this run; delete if you want only sourced facts.

Figlia G.role: Cell biologist who studied how mTORC1 senses nutrients in Aurelio Teleman's group at the German Cancer Research Center, including the finding that glutamine is sensed through the kinase GCN2, and who now works at the Institute of Neuropathology in Aachen
Figlia G.sub: Institute of Neuropathology, RWTH Aachen University Hospital (2025–) · Division of Signal Transduction in Cancer and Metabolism (Aurelio Teleman), German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and Heidelberg University (papers 2020–2025) · Institute of Molecular Health Sciences (Ueli Suter), ETH Zurich (papers 2014–2018)
story: Gianluca Figlia appears on two Atlas studies about brakes on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The 2021 Cell paper (PRE2021) found that G3BP1 and G3BP2, proteins best known from stress granules, also sit on the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment where mTORC1 is switched on. There they hold the TSC complex, the main off-switch for mTORC1, in place. Without them mTORC1 reacts too strongly to amino acids and insulin. The 2023 Nature Cell Biology paper (NIC2023) showed that malonyl-CoA, a building block made on the way to new fatty acids, fits into the same pocket of mTOR that normally holds ATP and so blocks it. When a cell cannot make fat fast enough, malonyl-CoA rises and slows mTORC1 down. Both results come mainly from cells; the first adds zebrafish experiments, and the second shows the malonyl-CoA effect is conserved across species.

Figlia's path ran through two labs that both linked mTOR to lipids. At ETH Zurich, in Ueli Suter's group, Figlia was second author of a 2014 Cell Reports paper showing in mice that mTORC1 in Schwann cells, the cells that wrap nerves in insulating myelin, drives myelin growth by switching on fat-making genes through SREBP. At the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, in Aurelio Teleman's group, Figlia was first author of a 2020 review on how metabolites control signalling by attaching chemically to proteins, and first author of a 2025 EMBO Journal paper showing that cells sense glutamine for mTORC1 entirely through the kinase GCN2, triggered by the loss of asparagine.
The 2025 paper and a 2026 commentary on TDP-43 disease list Figlia at the Institute of Neuropathology, RWTH Aachen University Hospital.

highlights.PRE2021: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that G3BP1 and G3BP2 tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and so hold mTORC1 in check.
highlights.NIC2023: Co-author: contributed from the DKFZ to the study showing that malonyl-CoA binds the mTOR catalytic pocket and inhibits mTORC1.

Figlia G.note: NIC2023 received an Author Correction (Nat Cell Biol, Oct 2026, PMID 42918817); not a retraction, just flagging. Current position from PubMed affiliations only (Aachen, 2025-2026); title not confirmed.

Beckers J.lab_name: Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic, Helmholtz Munich (Neuherberg, Germany)
Beckers J.role: Geneticist at Helmholtz Munich and the Technical University of Munich whose group at the Institute of Experimental Genetics runs gene-expression profiling for the German Mouse Clinic
Beckers J.sub: Institute of Experimental Genetics and German Mouse Clinic, Helmholtz Munich · Chair of Experimental Genetics, Technical University of Munich, Freising · German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD)
story: Johannes Beckers is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Beckers works at the Institute of Experimental Genetics of Helmholtz Munich in Neuherberg, near Munich, and PubMed records also list the Chair of Experimental Genetics at the Technical University of Munich and the German Center for Diabetes Research. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. In both Atlas papers Beckers appears among the German Mouse Clinic authors. Beckers's own papers centre on measuring which genes are switched on in tissues, for example with Marion Horsch and Martin Irmler, and range from mouse genetics to the effects of air pollution on the lung, as in a 2026 study of wood-smoke aerosols.

highlights.EIS2016: Co-author from the German Mouse Clinic, which contributed phenotyping to the mouse spermidine study.
highlights.NEF2013: Co-author from the German Mouse Clinic on the broad phenotyping that showed rapamycin changes only a few ageing traits in mice.

Beckers J.note: Specific role in the two papers (expression profiling) not stated in the abstracts; story keeps it general. No official profile page opened (web search budget ran out).

Pyo JO.lab_name: Yong-Keun Jung laboratory, School of Biological Sciences and Bio-MAX Institute, Seoul National University (Seoul, South Korea)
Pyo JO.role: Autophagy researcher in Yong-Keun Jung's group in Korea, and first author of the 2013 study in which mice with an extra dose of the autophagy gene Atg5 lived longer
Pyo JO.sub: Global Research Laboratory, School of Biological Sciences and Bio-MAX Institute, Seoul National University (papers 2008–2013, at the time of the study) · Department of Life Science, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (papers to 2005)
story: Jong-Ok Pyo was first author of a 2013 Nature Communications paper (PYO2013) that tested a simple idea. Autophagy is the cell's self-cleaning system: it wraps worn-out parts in a membrane bag and sends them to be broken down. Autophagy fades with age, and mTOR, the cell's growth switch, holds it back when nutrients are plentiful. The team made mice that carry extra copies of Atg5, one of the core genes needed to build the autophagy bags. These mice had more autophagy, lived about 17 percent longer at the median, stayed leaner and responded better to insulin, and their cells coped better with oxidative damage.
It showed that turning autophagy up, without blocking mTOR, can lengthen life in a mammal. It is a mouse study, and it does not show that the same would happen in people.

Pyo spent the earlier part of this path in the group of Yong-Keun Jung, first at the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology and then at Seoul National University. A 2005 first-author paper in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, written with the autophagy researchers Noboru Mizushima and Yoshinori Ohsumi among the co-authors, showed that Atg5 also takes part in a form of cell death by binding the death-signalling protein FADD. A 2008 first-author paper showed that extra ARC protein protects mouse heart muscle cells from damage when oxygen is cut off, and a 2012 review in Experimental & Molecular Medicine summarised the molecules that drive autophagy. No PubMed record after 2013 was found, and a current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.PYO2013: First author: showed that mice carrying extra Atg5 have more autophagy, live about 17 percent longer and are leaner and more insulin sensitive.

Pyo JO.note: Current position unknown; no publications after 2013 in PubMed. Ohsumi's name is misspelled 'Oshumi' in the PubMed record of PMID 15778222.

B'chir W.lab_name: Vincent Giguère laboratory, Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
B'chir W.role: Metabolism researcher in Vincent Giguère's laboratory at McGill who studies how the nuclear receptor ERR-alpha controls fat handling in the liver, including the fatty liver caused by rapamycin
B'chir W.sub: Goodman Cancer Institute, McGill University, Montreal (papers 2018–2026) · INRA Human Nutrition Unit and Université Clermont 1, Clermont-Ferrand, France (papers to 2013)
story: Wafa B'chir was first author of a 2026 Journal of Endocrinology study (BCH2026) on a side effect of rapamycin. Rapamycin blocks mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and is used to prevent organ rejection. In mice it can also cause fatty liver, where fat builds up inside liver cells. The team added chloroquine, an old antimalarial drug, and found that it made the rapamycin-induced fatty liver milder. Measuring all the genes switched on in the liver showed that chloroquine undid much of rapamycin's push on fat-handling genes, and the nuclear receptor ERR-alpha, a master switch for energy metabolism, came out as a top controller. In mice lacking ERR-alpha, chloroquine no longer helped. This is a mouse study, and it does not show that the combination is safe or useful in patients.

B'chir came to this from nutrition and stress biology. In 2013, at the INRA Human Nutrition Unit in Clermont-Ferrand, France, B'chir was first author of a Nucleic Acids Research paper showing that when amino acids run out, the GCN2 and PERK stress kinases act through ATF4 and CHOP to switch on a whole set of autophagy genes. At McGill's Goodman Cancer Research Centre B'chir moved to the liver: a 2018 first-author paper in Endocrinology found that mice without ERR-alpha are protected from fatty liver on a high-fat diet but cannot clear fat from the liver normally when fed again after fasting.
B'chir has continued with the Giguère group at the Goodman Cancer Institute on work about ERR-alpha in the heart (2022) and in the progression of fatty liver to liver inflammation in mice (2023).

highlights.BCH2026: First author: showed in mice that chloroquine softens rapamycin-induced fatty liver and that this rescue needs ERR-alpha.

B'chir W.note: Position title at McGill not confirmed (PubMed affiliations only). Link INRA 2013 to McGill rests on rare name plus autophagy/nutrient-stress topic.

St-Pierre J.lab_name: Ottawa Institute of Systems Biology and Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology, University of Ottawa (Ottawa, Ontario, Canada)
St-Pierre J.role: Biochemist at the University of Ottawa who studies how cells control their mitochondria and energy metabolism, and a co-author on McGill work linking mTORC1 to mitochondria and to rapamycin-induced fatty liver
St-Pierre J.sub: Ottawa Institute of Systems Biology and Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology, University of Ottawa · Goodman Cancer Research Centre and Department of Biochemistry, McGill University, Montreal (papers 2013–2026)
story: Julie St-Pierre is a co-author on two Atlas studies from McGill University about mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and energy metabolism. The 2013 Cell Metabolism paper (MOR2013), led by Nahum Sonenberg's group, showed in cells that mTORC1 sets how many mitochondria a cell builds and how hard they work. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations. mTORC1 does this by releasing the brake that 4E-BP proteins put on the production of proteins the mitochondria need. This links the growth signal directly to the energy supply that growth needs.

The 2026 Journal of Endocrinology paper (BCH2026), from Vincent Giguère's group, is a mouse study. Rapamycin, which blocks mTORC1, can cause fatty liver, and adding the antimalarial drug chloroquine made that fatty liver milder. The rescue depended on ERR-alpha, a nuclear receptor that switches on many energy metabolism genes; in mice without it, chloroquine did not help.

St-Pierre worked for many years at McGill's Goodman Cancer Research Centre and Department of Biochemistry, where in 2018 St-Pierre was also a co-author on the study of how ERR-alpha shapes fatty liver on a high-fat diet. The 2026 paper lists St-Pierre at both the Goodman Cancer Institute and the University of Ottawa, in the Ottawa Institute of Systems Biology and the Department of Biochemistry, Microbiology and Immunology.

highlights.BCH2026: Co-author: contributed to the mouse study showing that chloroquine softens rapamycin-induced fatty liver through ERR-alpha.
highlights.MOR2013: Co-author: contributed to the cell study showing that mTORC1 controls mitochondrial biogenesis and activity through 4E-BP-dependent translation.

St-Pierre J.note: Training (PhD, postdoc) not confirmed in this run: web search budget ran out, and PubMed shows several St-Pierre J (e.g. Jean-Philippe St-Pierre, Ottawa engineering). Position title at Ottawa not confirmed; from 2026 PubMed affiliation only. Consider adding an official uOttawa profile URL.

Hafez SA.lab_name: Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health (Abha, Saudi Arabia)
Hafez SA.role: Researcher with the Aseer Health Cluster in Abha, Saudi Arabia, and first author of a 2026 mouse study testing the bee-venom peptide melittin against psoriasis-like skin inflammation
Hafez SA.sub: Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, Saudi Ministry of Health, Abha (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Saeed A Hafez was first author of a 2026 Saudi Pharmaceutical Journal study (HAFEZ2026) on psoriasis, a common skin disease in which skin cells grow too fast and the skin becomes red, thick and scaly. The team produced a psoriasis-like rash in mice by rubbing imiquimod cream on the skin, a standard laboratory model. They then injected melittin, the main active peptide of bee venom. At the higher dose the rash score fell by about 60 percent.

The study links the effect to the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, the chain of signals that tells cells to grow. Melittin lowered the activity of this pathway in the skin and raised markers of autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system that mTOR normally holds back. This is one mouse model, with melittin given by injection into the abdomen, so it does not show that bee venom or melittin would help people with psoriasis.

PubMed lists Hafez at the Health Holding Company, Aseer Health Cluster, part of the Saudi Ministry of Health, in Abha. No other publication could be tied to this author with confidence, and a fuller career history could not be confirmed.

highlights.HAFEZ2026: First author: tested melittin in a mouse model of psoriasis and linked the lower rash score to reduced PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling and more autophagy.

Hafez SA.note: Other 'Hafez SA' records in PubMed with Abha/Aseer terms are different people (Sarah Ali Hafez, Alexandria nursing; Shahad A Hafez, Batterjee Medical College). Nothing else confirmed for Saeed A Hafez.

Lee DJW.lab_name: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (Singapore)
Lee DJW.role: First author of the first systematic review of rapamycin and related drugs given to people for ageing, from the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program at the National University of Singapore
Lee DJW.sub: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (at the time of the study, 2024)
story: Deborah J W Lee was first author of a 2024 systematic review in The Lancet Healthy Longevity (LEE2024). A systematic review gathers every study that meets fixed rules and judges them together, which makes it stronger than any single trial. The team screened about 18,400 records and kept 19 studies in which people took rapamycin or a related drug (a rapalog) with ageing-related outcomes in mind. The authors describe it as the first systematic review of its kind.

The picture was mixed. Measures of the immune system, the heart and blood vessels, and the skin improved in some studies. Hormone, muscle and brain measures showed no clear change. Healthy people had no serious side effects, but people who already had age-related diseases had more infections and higher cholesterol and triglycerides. For the Atlas this is one of the strongest summaries of what rapamycin does in humans, and it also shows how few human studies there are.

The paper lists Lee at the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program of the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore. No other publication could be tied to this author with confidence, and a current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.LEE2024: First author: led the systematic review of 19 human studies of rapamycin and rapalogs for ageing, which found gains in immune, cardiovascular and skin measures but none for hormones, muscle or the nervous system.

Lee DJW.note: A Deborah J W Lee at Changi General Hospital, Department of Laboratory Medicine (2023, PMID 37627966, co-author Tar-Choon Aw also NUS) may be the same person, but common surname and no shared co-author, so left out.

Demir A.lab_name: Simon Raffel group, Heidelberg University and Heidelberg University Hospital (Heidelberg, Germany)
Demir A.role: Leukaemia researcher at Heidelberg University and first author of the 2026 study showing that the enzyme IDH3 keeps acute myeloid leukaemia stem cells metabolically fit and resistant to venetoclax
Demir A.sub: Heidelberg University, Heidelberg (Simon Raffel group, at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Aykut Demir was first author of a 2026 paper in Blood (DEM2026) about acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), a fast-growing blood cancer. AML returns after treatment because a small group of leukaemic stem cells survives. These cells depend on the TCA cycle, the chain of reactions in mitochondria that burns fuel for energy, more than healthy blood stem cells do. The team found that the enzyme IDH3, one step of that cycle, is more abundant in leukaemic stem cells.

When they lowered IDH3A, the working part of the enzyme, citrate piled up inside the cells and both main energy pathways slowed. The resulting energy shortage switched on AMPK, the cell's fuel gauge, which shut down mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and so cut protein production. The cells then became more sensitive to venetoclax, a drug that blocks the survival protein BCL2. Healthy blood formation was spared. The work used patient cells, bone marrow organoids (miniature lab-grown tissue) and mice, and in a patient group, stem cells from people whose leukaemia resisted venetoclax plus azacitidine showed gene programmes of an active TCA cycle.

The paper lists Demir at Heidelberg University, in a team led by Simon Raffel at Heidelberg University Hospital with Andreas Trumpp of the German Cancer Research Center and Carsten Müller-Tidow among the co-authors. Other PubMed records under the same initials belong to different people, and a fuller career history could not be confirmed.

highlights.DEM2026: First author: showed that loss of IDH3A in AML stem cells raises citrate, activates AMPK and shuts down mTORC1, making the cells more sensitive to venetoclax.

Demir A.note: Other 'Demir A' PubMed records (Trakya hematology, Ankara pediatrics) are different people. Position title not confirmed.

Cao Z.lab_name: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University (Harbin, China)
Cao Z.role: Veterinary toxicologist at Northeast Agricultural University in Harbin whose group studies how pollutants and food toxins damage the kidney, liver and gut in mice
Cao Z.sub: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin
story: Zheng Cao was senior author of a 2026 Environmental Science & Technology study (MIAO2026) on EDPrB, a liquid-crystal monomer, one of the chemicals used in flat screens that can leak into the environment. In mice, EDPrB built up in the kidney and caused chronic kidney disease. The team traced the harm to overactive mTOR, the cell's growth switch. When mTOR stays on, autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, is held back, and the kidney developed inflammation and fibrosis, a stiff scar tissue. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, prevented the damage, which marked mTOR activation as the first step in the chain. Human kidney cells grown in a dish gave matching results.

The study is written as an adverse outcome pathway, a step-by-step map from the first molecular hit to disease that toxicologists use to judge chemical risks. It is evidence from mice and cultured cells, not from exposed people.

Cao's group at the Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine in Harbin works on how contaminants injure organs. Recent papers from the group show that the mycotoxin deoxynivalenol, a common contaminant of grain, breaks down the gut barrier (2024) and harms the liver through excessive mitophagy, the removal of mitochondria (2025), that the plastic chemical bisphenol F causes kidney inflammation and fibrosis through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum (2026), and that a berberine gel can ease mastitis in a mouse model (2026).

highlights.MIAO2026: Senior author: led the mouse and cell study showing that the pollutant EDPrB causes kidney disease through mTOR overactivation, which rapamycin prevented.

Cao Z.note: Position title not confirmed (PubMed affiliations only). Common surname; all papers tied by the same Harbin laboratory and shared co-authors (Miao C, Zhang B, Yu W).

Miao C.lab_name: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University (Harbin, China)
Miao C.role: Researcher in Zheng Cao's group at Northeast Agricultural University who studies how environmental and food toxins damage organs in mice, and first author of the 2026 study tying a screen chemical to kidney disease through mTOR
Miao C.sub: Heilongjiang Key Laboratory for Laboratory Animals and Comparative Medicine, College of Veterinary Medicine, Northeast Agricultural University, Harbin (papers 2024–2026)
story: Chenjiao Miao was first author of a 2026 Environmental Science & Technology study (MIAO2026) on EDPrB, a liquid-crystal monomer used in display screens that can escape into the environment. Mice exposed to EDPrB built it up in the kidney and developed chronic kidney disease. The chain of harm started with overactive mTOR, the cell's growth switch. With mTOR stuck on, autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was suppressed, and inflammation and fibrosis, a stiff scar tissue, followed. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, prevented the damage, and human kidney cells in a dish responded in the same way.

The paper lays this out as an adverse outcome pathway, a step-by-step map that regulators can use to judge chemical risk. It shows a mechanism in mice and cells; it does not measure harm in exposed people.

Miao works in Zheng Cao's group in Harbin. Earlier first-author work showed in mice and pig gut cells that the grain mycotoxin deoxynivalenol damages the intestinal barrier through the RhoA/ROCK pathway (2024), and a 2026 first-author paper found that the plastic chemical bisphenol F drives kidney inflammation and fibrosis through stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and changes in kidney macrophages.

highlights.MIAO2026: First author: showed in mice and human kidney cells that the pollutant EDPrB causes kidney disease through mTOR overactivation and suppressed autophagy.

Miao C.note: Career stage (student or staff) not confirmed.

Vitte SH.lab_name: Hospital de Amor Nossa Senhora (Barretos, Brazil)
Vitte SH.role: Brazilian medical researcher who works on evidence synthesis and cardiometabolic studies, and first author of the 2026 meta-analysis of everolimus in heart transplant recipients
Vitte SH.sub: Hospital de Amor Nossa Senhora, Barretos (VITTE2026, 2026) · Department of Medicine, Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Campinas (2025–2026) · Atherosclerosis and Vascular Biology Laboratory (Aterolab), State University of Campinas (2022–2024)
story: Sofia Helena Vitte was first author of a 2026 meta-analysis in JHLT Open (VITTE2026) on everolimus after heart transplantation. Everolimus is a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTOR and is used to stop the immune system from attacking a new organ. A meta-analysis pools the numbers from many studies to get a clearer answer than any one study gives. This one pooled 60 studies with 1,786 heart transplant recipients.

Everolimus-based treatment slowed cardiac allograft vasculopathy, the narrowing of the transplanted heart's arteries that limits how long the new heart lasts, to about 57 percent of the risk seen without it. When doctors also reduced calcineurin inhibitors, older drugs that damage the kidneys, kidney function was clearly better. Deaths from any cause did not change, but side effects and stopping treatment were more common. This is evidence from transplant patients, pooled across studies of different designs.

PubMed shows Vitte's earlier work at the Atherosclerosis and Vascular Biology Laboratory of the State University of Campinas, on the Brazilian Diabetes Study of people with type 2 diabetes (2022 to 2024), and later at the Department of Medicine of the Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Campinas, including other meta-analyses on exercise after Fontan heart surgery (2025) and on preventing lung collapse after CT-guided lung biopsy (2026). The 2026 everolimus paper lists the Hospital de Amor Nossa Senhora in Barretos.

highlights.VITTE2026: First author: led the meta-analysis of 60 studies showing that everolimus slows transplant artery disease and protects kidney function in heart recipients, without changing mortality.

Vitte SH.note: Identity tie Unicamp -> PUC-Campinas -> Barretos: rare name, and senior author G.M. Munaretto is shared by VITTE2026 and the 2026 Clinical Radiology meta-analysis (PUC-Campinas affiliation). Career stage (student or physician) not confirmed. 'about 57 percent of the risk' paraphrases RR ~0.57; adjust if preferred.

Huang RK.lab_name: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus (Ashburn, Virginia, USA)
Huang RK.role: Cryo-electron microscopy specialist who, at the HHMI Janelia Research Campus, helped solve the 2018 and 2019 structures of the protein machines that pass amino acid signals to mTORC1
Huang RK.sub: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Janelia Research Campus, Ashburn, Virginia (at the time of the studies, 2018–2019)
story: Rick K. Huang is a co-author on two Atlas studies from David Sabatini's laboratory, led by Kuang Shen, that used cryo-electron microscopy to see how amino acid signals reach mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Cryo-EM freezes purified proteins in thin ice and builds a 3D model from many thousands of electron microscope images. The Rag GTPases are a pair of switch proteins on the lysosome surface that pull mTORC1 there when amino acids are present.

The 2018 Nature paper (SHE2018) showed the shape of GATOR1, the complex that switches the Rags off when amino acids are scarce, alone and bound to the Rags. It revealed both the part that speeds up the Rags' GTP burning and a second, unexpected grip that holds them in place. The 2019 Cell paper (SHE2019) showed folliculin with its partner FNIP2 sitting on the Rags and on Ragulator, the platform that anchors them to the lysosome. Both studies used purified human proteins and biochemical tests, not cells or animals.
Both papers list Huang at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus in Ashburn, Virginia. A current position could not be confirmed with certainty.

highlights.SHE2018: Co-author from Janelia: contributed to the cryo-EM structures of GATOR1 alone and bound to the Rag GTPases.
highlights.SHE2019: Co-author from Janelia: contributed to the cryo-EM structure of the FLCN-FNIP2-Rag-Ragulator complex.

Huang RK.note: PubMed lists a Rick K Huang doing cryo-EM at NIH (NICHD Unit on Structural Biology, 2022, PMID 36514310; NCI Laboratory of Cell Biology, 2026, PMID 42896292). Very likely the same person (same full name and middle initial, same technique), but common surname and no shared co-author with the Atlas papers, so not in the text. Exact role at Janelia (cryo-EM facility) not confirmed; SHE2018 detail (GAP plus inhibitory clamp) comes from the Atlas finding.
